name: Midsummer

attributes.attribute: a Celtic calendar festival marking the start of summer
falls on June 21, the summer solstice
a time of dancing, feasting, fern seed, and portents
linked to fortune telling for young women

sources: Briggs, Katharine M. The Folklore of the Cotswolds. London: B. T. Batsford Ltd., 1974, 14.
Hunt, Robert. Cornish Customs and Superstitions. Truro: Tor Mark Press, n.d.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Midsummer was a calendar festival of the Celts. The Celts did not mark the solstices, the longest and shortest days, nor the equinoxes, the days of equal light and dark. They marked the days at the center of each season, such as Imbolc, Beltane, Lughnasa, and Samhain. As they met earlier peoples who used the solar pivot points as calendar feasts, they took up rituals for those days. The change from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar moved some old holidays from their original dates, so some Lughnasa harvest rituals became midsummer festivals near the end of June. Midsummer itself is not the middle of summer. It is the season's start on June 21, when the sun is closest to the northern hemisphere and night is much shorter than day. In Scotland and Ireland daylight lasted long into the evening, and so dancing and feasting were common. Girls in England went to stone circles and whispered the names of favored young men to the stones, which were said to tell the future on that day. People gathered fern seed for potions of invisibility and sowed hemp to see portents. In Cornwall girls left their underwear turned inside out and watched at midnight for a ghostly form to turn it right, and so learn the names of their future husbands. Or they could pluck a rose, keep it until Christmas, and wear it to church, where the faded rose would attract the groom to be.
